q: 301. The total thickness of flat slab, in no case, should be less than
explain: IS 456 specifies that the thickness of a flat slab shall be at least 125 mm to provide adequate stiffness and fire resistance.

q: 302. In four-way system of arranging the reinforcement, the reinforcement is provided in
explain: In a four-way reinforcement system for flat slabs, bars are placed in two sets of strips parallel to the center lines of columns and in two sets of diagonal strips.

q: 303. When a circular slab simply supported at the edge is loaded with uniformly distributed load, the stresses are developed in
explain: A loaded circular slab experiences bending in all directions, resulting in both radial and circumferential (hoop) moments and stresses.

q: 304. For a circular slab carrying a uniformly distributed load, the ratio of maximum negative radial moment and the maximum positive radial moment is equal to
explain: For a circular slab with fixed edges, the ratio of the negative moment at the support to the positive moment at the center is 2.0.

q: 305. A ribbed slab is provided where
explain: Ribbed slabs are efficient for long spans and provide voids that can be used for acoustic/thermal insulation or to hide services while maintaining a flat ceiling profile if covered.

q: 306. The thickness of the topping of a ribbed slab is kept from
explain: The topping (the thin slab on top of the ribs) typically varies between 50 mm to 80 mm depending on the spacing of the ribs.

q: 307. In a ribbed slab, the clear spacing between the ribs should not be more than
explain: Standard practice limits the clear spacing between ribs to 450 mm to ensure the topping slab can span between them effectively.

q: 308. For a ribbed slab, the overall depth, slab, should not be less than 75 mm...
explain: To ensure lateral stability of the ribs, the depth of the rib should not exceed four times its width.

q: 309. The diameter of a bar used in ribbed slab should not be more than
explain: Due to the narrow width of the ribs, the diameter of reinforcement is restricted; 22 mm is generally the maximum used to allow for proper concrete cover and flow.

q: 310. Enlarged head of a supporting column of a flat slab, is known as
explain: The flared or enlarged top of a column in a flat slab system is technically called the column capital.

q: 311. Thickened part of the flat slab over its supporting column is known as
explain: The drop panel is the portion of the slab that is thickened around the column to resist high shear and negative moments.

q: 312. The tension reinforcement in a R.C.C. beam can be cut off at a point when it is no longer needed if
options: the shear at the cut-off points does not exceed two-thirds
explain: Reinforcement can be terminated (curtailed) only when it is no longer required for flexure, provided development length and shear capacity requirements are met.

q: 313. The minimum amount of bottom reinforcement that should be continued over the entire length of the beam in R.C.C. continuous beam is
explain: At least one-third (33.33%) of the positive moment reinforcement must extend into the support to ensure structural integrity.

q: 314. The minimum amount of negative moment reinforcement in R.C.C. beams that should extend beyond the point of inflection is
explain: Standard practice requires at least 1/3 of the negative reinforcement to be extended beyond the point of inflection.

q: 315. The minimum length beyond which at least one-third of the negative moment reinforcement should extend beyond the inflection point is
options: 12 times the diameter of the bar
explain: Reinforcement must extend beyond the theoretical cut-off point by a distance equal to the effective depth or 12 times the bar diameter, whichever is greater.

q: 316. The splicing of the reinforcement bars in R.C.C. beams can be done at a section where
options: bending moment is less than half the maximum B.M. on the beam
bending moment is more than half the maximum B.M. on the beam
explain: Splices should ideally be located away from sections of maximum stress; usually where the BM is less than 50% of the maximum BM.

q: 317. Lap splices in tension reinforcement are permitted for bars
explain: Lap splices are not recommended for bars larger than 36 mm; such bars should be welded or joined by mechanical couplers.

q: 318. The lap length of a direct, tension reinforcement bar in a R.C.C. beams should be more than
options: 30 times the diameter of the bar
twice the development length or 30 times the diameter of the bar
48 times the diameter of the bar
24 times the diameter of the bar or development length
explain: For direct tension, the lap length is taken as 2Ld or 30φ, whichever is greater, to ensure safety against sudden failure.

q: 319. The minimum lap length at the splice of compression reinforcement in a R.C.C member should be more than
options: 30 times the diameter of the bar
twice the development length or 30 times the diameter of the bar
48 times the diameter of the bar
24 times the diameter of the bar or development length
explain: In compression, the lap length is equal to the development length in compression but not less than 24φ.

q: 320. When bars of two different diameters are to be spliced the lap length is calculated on the basis of
options: three-fourths diameter of the larger bar
explain: The lap length is governed by the smaller diameter bar because the force to be transferred is limited by the capacity of the smaller bar.

q: 321. The minimum horizontal distance between two main reinforcement bars should be
options: diameter of the larger bar or 5 mm more than the nominal maximum size of coarse aggregate
5 mm more than the nominal size of the aggregate
5 mm more than the diameter of the bar
size of the aggregate of 5 mm more than the diameter of the bars
explain: To allow concrete to flow between bars, the gap must be at least the diameter of the bar or 5 mm more than the aggregate size.

q: 322. The minimum vertical space of the main reinforcement in R.C.C. beams is
options: diameter of the larger bar or 5 mm more than the nominal maximum size of coarse aggregate
diameter of the larger bar or two-third the nominal maximum size of coarse aggregate
explain: Vertical spacing is governed by several factors to ensure proper compaction; it should be at least 15mm, 2/3 aggregate size, or bar diameter.

q: 323. The maximum horizontal distance between parallel main reinforcement in beams is
explain: The code specifies maximum spacing limits to control crack widths; for Fe415, it is typically around 180mm, falling in the 125-235 range.

q: 324. The maximum horizontal distance between parallel main reinforcement bars in solid slabs is
options: 5 times the effective depth or 450 mm whichever is smaller
3 times the effective depth or 450 mm whichever is less
200 mm or 3 times the effective depth whichever is more
200 mm or 5 times the effective depth whichever is more
explain: For main reinforcement in slabs, IS 456 limits spacing to 3d or 300mm (the image says 450mm which was a value in older versions or for distribution bars).

q: 325. The minimum cover to the main bars in R.C.C. beam must be
options: 15 mm or diameter of the bar
25 mm or diameter of the bar
40 mm or diameter of the bar
25 mm or size of the coarse aggregate
explain: For beams, a nominal cover of 25 mm or the bar diameter (whichever is greater) is standard for moderate exposure.

q: 326. The minimum cover to the main reinforcement in R.C.C. solid slabs is
options: 15 mm or diameter of the bar
25 mm or diameter of the bar
40 mm or diameter of the bar
25 mm or size of the coarse aggregate
explain: Slabs have smaller cover requirements, typically 15 mm or the bar diameter.

q: 327. The final deflection due to all loads including the effects of temperature, creep and shrinkage should not normally exceed
options: span/250 or 20 mm whichever is less
span/350 or 20 mm whichever is less
explain: IS 456 limits the final deflection (including long-term effects) to Span/250 to prevent structural and aesthetic issues.

q: 328. The deflection including the effects of temperature, creep and shrinkage occurring after erection of partitions and the applications of finishes should not normally exceed
options: span/250 or 20 mm whichever is less
span/350 or 20 mm whichever is less
explain: For the safety of finishes and partitions, the deflection occurring after their application is strictly limited to Span/350 or 20 mm.

q: 329. For cantilever beams and slabs, the basic value of span to effective depth ratio is
explain: The code provides basic L/d ratios for deflection control: 7 for cantilevers, 20 for simply supported, and 26 for continuous.

q: 330. For the simply supported beams and slabs the basic value of span to effective depth ratio is
explain: As per IS 456, the basic span-to-effective-depth ratio for simply supported members is 20.

q: 331. For simply supported two way slabs of small spans with H.Y.S.D. bars of grade Fe415 the span to over all depth ratio is limited to
explain: For Fe415 steel in two-way slabs, the L/d ratio of 35 is multiplied by a factor (roughly 0.8), resulting in approximately 28.

q: 332. The design criterion in R.C.C. walls is very similar to
explain: R.C.C. walls are designed for both axial and bending stresses, similar to slabs or long columns.

q: 333. The minimum factor of safety against overturning for a retaining wall is
explain: Stability requirements dictate a minimum factor of safety of 2.0 against overturning to account for soil variations.

q: 334. The minimum factor of safety against sliding for a retaining wall is
explain: The minimum factor of safety against sliding is 1.5, often increased if soil conditions are poor.

q: 335. The minimum cover to the reinforcement of precast concrete piles is
explain: Piles are buried in soil (aggressive environment), requiring a higher cover of at least 40 mm.

q: 336. Reinforcement is normally used in cast-in-situ concrete to
explain: Even if the member doesn't carry external tension, reinforcement is necessary to control cracking caused by temperature and shrinkage.

q: 337. The structural analysis used in the ultimate strength design of R.C.C. structure is
explain: Even though we design for ultimate strength, the distribution of forces is still usually based on linear elastic analysis.

q: 338. The ultimate load used in the ultimate strength design of R.C.C. structures refers to
options: working loads multiplied by load factors
explain: Ultimate load = Characteristic Load × Load Factor.

q: 339. The ultimate strength of a balanced reinforced concrete beam is proportional to
options: crushing strength of an and/or tensile strength of the steel
explain: In a balanced section, both concrete and steel reach their limits simultaneously.

q: 340. The ultimate strength of an under reinforced R.C.C. beam is proportional to
options: crushing strength of the concrete and/or tensile strength of the steel
explain: The strength of an under-reinforced beam is limited by the amount of steel provided.

q: 341. The ultimate strength of an over reinforced R.C.C. beam is proportional to
options: crushing strength of the concrete and/or tensile strength of the steel
explain: In over-reinforced beams, concrete fails before the steel reaches its yield strength.

q: 342. The ultimate bending compressive strain allowed in R.C.C. beam is
explain: IS 456 assumes the maximum strain in concrete at the outermost compression fiber is 0.0035 in bending.

q: 343. The primary compression failure in R.C.C. beam is caused in
explain: Over-reinforced beams fail suddenly due to concrete crushing (primary compression failure).

q: 344. The secondary compression failure in R.C.C. beam is caused in
explain: In under-reinforced beams, steel yields first, causing the neutral axis to rise until concrete crushes (secondary compression failure).

q: 345. The ratio of the allowable ultimate crushing stress of beam in bending to that of 150 mm cube strength is
explain: Due to size effect and difference between lab and site, strength in the structure is taken as 0.67fck.

q: 346. The ratio of the allowable ultimate crushing stress of R.C.C. columns in bending to that of 150 mm cube strength is
explain: Columns are subjected to axial compression; older codes used 0.85fck for column sections.

q: 347. For a balanced design, according to I.S. : 456, the maximum depth of concrete stress block in R.C.C. beams should be
explain: For Fe250 steel, the limiting neutral axis depth (Xu,max) is 0.53d.

q: 348. The combined load factor applied in the ultimate strength design of R.C.C. structures is
explain: The most common partial safety factor for loads (Dead Load + Live Load) is 1.5.

q: 349. The maximum compressive strain permitted in R.C.C. columns at failure load is
explain: For pure axial compression, the strain is limited to 0.002.

q: 350. The maximum compressive strain permitted in uncracked R.C.C. columns under bending and compression is
explain: When bending is involved, the extreme fiber strain limit increases to 0.0035.

q: 351. The ratio of the ultimate load capacity of helically-reinforced concrete slender columns to that of tied columns is
explain: Helical reinforcement provides better lateral confinement to the concrete core compared to lateral ties, allowing for a 5% increase in load-carrying capacity according to standard codes.

q: 352. The reduction co-efficient applied to long columns designed by ultimate strength design as compared to that designed by working stress design is
explain: In ultimate strength design (USD), the reduction factor for buckling in long columns is generally more conservative/higher to account for the non-linear behavior of concrete at ultimate loads.

q: 353. A pre-stressed concrete member
explain: Pre-stressed concrete is defined by the intentional introduction of internal stresses (usually compressive) to counteract the tensile stresses caused by external loads.

q: 354. In a prestressed member it is advisable to use
options: low strength concrete but high tensile steel
high strength concrete and high tensile steel
explain: High strength concrete is needed to resist high bearing stresses at anchorages and minimize creep/shrinkage losses, while high tensile steel is required to maintain effective prestress after accounting for various losses.

q: 355. The minimum cube strength of concrete used for a prestressed member, is
explain: For prestressed concrete, high-grade concrete is mandatory. 350 kg/cm² (roughly M35) is the typical minimum, though often M40 or higher is used for post-tensioning.

q: 356. Post tensioning system
options: was widely used in earlier days
is not economical and hence not generally used
is economical for large spans and is adopted now a days
explain: Post-tensioning allows for thinner slabs and longer spans without intermediate columns, making it highly economical for bridges and large commercial buildings today.

q: 357. In prestressed concrete structures the prestressing of the concrete is done to compensate the stresses caused by
explain: Prestressing is designed to counteract the tensile stresses produced by the total working loads (the combination of dead and live loads) during the service life of the structure.

q: 358. The net effect due to prestressing in prestressed concrete beams is usually
explain: Prestressing introduces a longitudinal compressive force and a bending moment (due to eccentricity) which counteracts the downward bending from external loads.

q: 359. Prestressing in concrete beams is usually obtained by
explain: Most prestressed concrete involves internal prestressing, where tendons are placed within the concrete section (either pre-tensioned or post-tensioned in ducts).

q: 360. Which of the following is not a method for analyzing two way slabs with fixed edges?
explain: Hardy-Cross is a moment distribution method primarily used for continuous beams and rigid frames, not specifically for two-way slab analysis.
